news.title: Can Democrats flip the Senate in the 2026 US midterms?
news.text:
With election day set for November 3, the United States enters the final month of the 2026 midterm election campaign.
Following the 2024 presidential elections, Republicans established a 53-seat majority in the upper chamber of Congress, leaving Democrats with 45 seats alongside two independents who caucus with them, giving the minority block an effective 47 votes.
To wrest control of the Senate away from Majority Leader Mitch McConnell’s successor and the Republican conference, Democrats must achieve a net gain of four seats.
Because US Vice President JD Vance provides Republicans with the tie-breaking vote in a 50-50 scenario, a simple 50-seat coalition is insufficient for Democrats, they require a clean 51-seat majority to take the gavel.
While flipping four seats in a single election cycle is an uphill battle under any circumstances, the electoral map this year offers Democrats their most favourable structural landscape in six years.
Of the 35 Senate seats on the ballot this November — consisting of 33 regularly scheduled Class 2 seats and two high-profile special elections — Republicans are forced to defend 22 seats, while Democrats are defending just 13.
The 2026 Class 2 Senate map is notable because it features seats that were last contested during the 2020 election, a cycle characterised by record turnout and national polarisation.
In that cycle, Democrats performed strongly in key suburban corridors, while Republicans solidified their grip on rural electorates.
Where are the Republicans most vulnerable?
Democrats have concentrated their resource allocation and national strategy on a small cluster of competitive Republican-held seats where local political trends give the challenger party a fighting chance.
North Carolina
North Carolina represents what many analysts regard as the Democratic Party's single best opportunity to pick up a Senate seat this November. The seat became open when Republican Senator Thom Tillis announced he would not seek reelection.
In response, national Democrats scored a major recruitment victory by convincing Roy Cooper, the immensely popular former two-term Democratic governor of North Carolina, to launch a Senate campaign.
Cooper enters the contest with a unique political record. He has never lost a statewide election in North Carolina across three decades of public service, having won two races for attorney general and two races for governor in years when Republican presidential candidates carried the state.
Cooper is facing Republican nominee Michael Whatley, the former chairman of the Republican National Committee and former head of the North Carolina Republican Party.
Whatley, who received the explicit endorsement of US President Donald Trump, has framed the race around national economic conditions and conservative policy priorities.
However, Cooper's high name recognition, moderate brand, and formidable fundraising coalition have consistently made North Carolina a top toss-up race in handicapper ratings from The Cook Political Report and Sabato's Crystal Ball.
In Maine, five-term Republican Senator Susan Collins is defending her seat in a state that Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 presidential election.
Collins holds the distinction of being the sole remaining Republican member of Congress from New England, as well as the only Senate Republican representing a state won by the Democratic presidential candidate in 2024.
Collins has built a career on defying national political gravity through localised constituency service and a reputation as a moderate swing vote. However, Democrats view her as increasingly vulnerable following recent Supreme Court rulings and key votes aligned with the Trump administration.
The Maine contest experienced upheaval earlier this summer. Progressive candidate Graham Platner, who had initially won traction among grassroots supporters, withdrew from the race in July following personal allegations.
Democratic leaders quickly rallied behind former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, a progressive union organiser and former logger.
Jackson's populist roots and blue-collar appeal in rural Northern Maine have reinvigorated the Democratic campaign, turning what looked like a comfortable lead for Collins into a hard-fought battle down the stretch.
One of the most watched races on the midterm map is the special election in Ohio to fill the final two years of the Senate term previously held by Vance.
Following Vance's inauguration, Republican Governor Mike DeWine appointed Lieutenant Governor Jon Husted to the vacant seat. Husted is now seeking to retain the seat in a high-stakes general election.
While Ohio has trended strongly toward Republicans in presidential elections over the past decade, Democrats produced a blockbuster candidate when former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown announced his return to politics.
Brown, who narrowly lost his seat in 2024 during a strong Republican wave year, remains one of the most durable Democratic figures in the Rust Belt.
Running on his signature "dignity of work" platform, Brown is leaning heavily into labour issues, domestic manufacturing, and consumer protections.
Husted, meanwhile, focuses on economic development and the state's conservative momentum under Republican governance. Brown's personal popularity makes Ohio a far more competitive landscape than the state's baseline political leaning would otherwise suggest.
For decades, winning a US Senate seat in Texas has been an elusive goal for Democrats, who last won a statewide election in the state in 1988. However, the 2026 contest has been reshaped by extraordinary primary battles on both sides of the aisle.
On the Republican side, longtime incumbent Senator John Cornyn faced a bruising primary runoff challenge from conservative Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Armed with an endorsement from Trump late in the primary campaign, Paxton defeated Cornyn, sending shockwaves through the establishment wing of the party.
Democrats nominated state Representative James Talarico, who emerged from a high-turnout primary victory over US Representative Jasmine Crockett.
Talarico, a former public school teacher and seminarian known for his articulate advocacy on public education and economic justice, offers Democrats a fresh messenger in Texas. While Texas remains a lean-Republican state on paper, national Democrats hope Paxton’s controversial legal history and polarising style will create an opening for an upset.
Iowa and Alaska
Beyond the top tier of targets, Democrats are eyeing secondary pickup opportunities in Iowa and Alaska.
In Iowa, two-term Republican Senator Joni Ernst announced her retirement in late 2025, creating an open-seat contest.
Republicans nominated Representative Ashley Hinson, while Democrats selected state Representative Josh Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medallist in wheelchair basketball who earned a prominent endorsement from former US President Barack Obama.
In Alaska, incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan faces a competitive challenge from former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola, whose nonpartisan brand and statewide popularity make Alaska one of the most unpredictable contests on the ballot.
Where are the Democrats most vulnerable?
While Democrats search for four pickup opportunities, they must simultaneously defend their own turf.
First-term Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is defending his seat in Georgia, making him the only Democratic senator running for reelection in 2026 in a state carried by Trump in the 2024 presidential race.
Ossoff, who won his seat in a dramatic 2021 runoff election, has built one of the most sophisticated fundraising and grassroots voter turnout organisations in the country.
Ossoff is facing Republican Representative Mike Collins, a conservative congressman who secured the Republican nomination with strong support from Trump.
Collins has centred his campaign on border security, federal spending, and linking Ossoff to national Democratic policies. Ossoff has countered by highlighting federal infrastructure investment in Georgia, veterans' care, and independent oversight on the Senate floor.
Given Georgia's narrow political margins, this race is expected to be among the most expensive per capita in modern Senate history.
In Michigan, three-term Democratic Senator Gary Peters announced he would not seek reelection, creating a high-stakes open-seat race in a critical Rust Belt swing state.
Michigan voted narrowly for Trump in 2024, making this open seat a top target for national Republicans.
Republicans nominated former Representative Mike Rogers, who ran a competitive Senate campaign in 2024 and retains strong statewide visibility.
On the Democratic side, a fiery primary culminated in a victory for progressive leader Abdul El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit health director who defeated moderate Representative Haley Stevens.
El-Sayed's campaign focuses heavily on Medicare for All, clean water infrastructure, and labor rights, while Rogers focuses on automotive industry jobs, trade policy, and inflation.
Who will win the Senate in 2026?
Midterm elections historically function as a referendum on the sitting presidential administration.
How voters evaluate Trump's second-term policies, executive actions, and judicial appointments will heavily influence independent turnout in battleground states.
Money continues to pour into the 2026 Senate battlegrounds at unprecedented levels.
Independent expenditure groups, party committees, and Super PACs associated with both parties have reserved hundreds of millions of dollars in television, digital, and ground-game advertising across key states.
In North Carolina, Georgia, Maine, and Ohio, advertising expenditures have already broken previous midterm records.
Democratic campaigns have drawn heavy support from small-dollar grassroots donors, enabling candidates like Jon Ossoff, Roy Cooper, and Sherrod Brown to post massive fundraising totals.
On the Republican side, strong support from major donor networks and national Super PACs has ensured that candidates like Michael Whatley, Mike Collins, and Ken Paxton remain fully funded heading into the final sprint.
For Democrats to reach 51 seats, their path requires executing a two-part strategy: holding every single one of their 13 seats on the ballot — including highly vulnerable contests in states carried by Trump — and netting four pickups from the 22 Republican-held seats up for election.
Early voting is already underway in several states as tens of millions of Americans prepare to cast their ballots.

news.title: The Patriot Post® · A Leaner Federal Workforce Is a Win for Taxpayers
news.text:
One of the most unheralded policy successes of President Donald Trump’s second term has been the purging of many unnecessary federal jobs.

The federal government has reduced its workforce by 300,000 jobs since Jan. 20, 2025, bringing it down to a still-bulky 2.7 million employees. Not since President Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society vastly expanded the scope of the national government has the federal workforce been at this level.

It’s not merely that the feds have shed superfluous jobs — there are still over 4 million contract workers, after all. It’s that the White House has been targeting all the right institutions.

The bloated War Department, with over 61,000 departures, and the equally bloated State Department, with 37% of its staff gone, experienced the biggest reductions.

But most of the buyouts were aimed at agencies and departments that should have been shuttered a long time ago. Take the U.S. Agency for International Development, which, for years, was used to funnel billions to hard-left ideological projects around the world. Virtually its entire staff is gone.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the unaccountable bureaucratic brainchild of progressive Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), has lost roughly 88% of its workers, though it’s still far too big.

The Agriculture Department, which, despite its name, is principally a welfare agency that has little to do with farming, experienced tens of thousands of departures. So has another welfare-state institution, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, whose most notable achievement has been helping inflate housing prices.

Not every agency is being clipped fast enough, though. Early in his term, Trump signed an executive order directing the dismantling of the Education Department. Yet this intrusive agency, which spends its time propping up unions and undermining local initiatives, has lost only 40% of its staff.

Every time Republicans threaten to cut federal jobs, though they rarely follow through, Democrats predict that society will be plunged into chaos and high unemployment.

The unemployment rate in September 2024 was 4.1%. In September 2025, it was 4.4%. It’s at 4.1% today. Barely anyone, one suspects, has noticed that the federal workforce has shrunk by around 11%. They probably wouldn’t notice if it shrank by another 11%.

What Democrats really fear is losing power. Federal agencies, government employees and public-sector unions are all bases of political influence for the Left.

“This is an attempt at intimidation,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) complained when the Office of Management and Budget released a memo instructing agencies to plan for large-scale layoffs. “Donald Trump has been firing federal workers since day one — not to govern, but to scare.”

Why would Democrats be “scared” of a leaner federal workforce?

We don’t know how government employees vote, but we can make an educated guess. Around 84% of campaign donations from federal workers went to Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024. Federal civilian jobs rose by over 130,000 under the Biden administration. Around 11% of the approximately 16 million jobs added during Biden’s term were federal, state and local government jobs. Roughly 15% of the total workforce, around 24 million people, still work for the government at all levels.

There is more that can be done, not only in trimming the federal workforce but also in decentralizing and dispersing it. The Trump administration promised to relocate more federal jobs out of the Washington area. The political class entrenched around the capital in Virginia and Maryland keeps voting to empower itself. It should be dispersed as much as possible. 

In 2001, anti-tax activist Grover Norquist famously proclaimed that his goal was to shrink the federal government until it was small enough to “drag it into the bathroom and drown it in the bathtub.” We’ve learned over the years that it doesn’t work that way. Neither party has any plan to curb spending, and voters don’t seem to be clamoring for one.

Shrinking the federal bureaucracy and workforce isn’t going to restrain massive deficit spending and our economy-threatening, turbocharged debt. Still, paring down the size, scope and intrusiveness of a swollen federal government, even if it’s just temporary until Democrats come back into power, is a win for taxpayers.

news.title: NY GOP Rep. Mike Lawler leads Dem Cait Conley in key battleground House district: new internal poll
news.text:
Hudson Valley Rep. Mike Lawler (R-NY) has pulled ahead of his Democratic rival Cait Conley by a narrow three points in the neck-and-neck battleground race, new internal polling shared exclusively with The Post shows.

The incumbent GOP pol leads with 50% of the vote compared with Conley’s 47% in the 17th Congressional District battle, according to the Lawler campaign’s internal poll of 400 likely voters, conducted Sept. 28 to 30.

The poll, administered by McLaughlin & Associates, has a margin of error of 4.9% — further evidence of the key race remaining a true toss-up.

The new survey comes a day after a PIX 11 and Emerson College poll showed Conley — a West Point grad and Biden administration national security official — with a razor-thin two-point lead over Lawler.

The Emerson-PIX 11 poll was conducted Sept. 27 to 29.

The Lawler campaign poll showed the second-term congressman up 92% to Conley’s 6% among Republicans, and up 52% to Conley’s 40% amongst independents.

It also shows Lawler with a considerable 20% of Democrats, to Conley’s 79%.

The 17th District, covering Westchester, Rockland, Putnam and Dutchess Counties, was carried by former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 and is one of Democrats’ most sought-after pickups in November’s midterm elections.

Lawler’s survey also included polling showing GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman leading Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul 51% to 47% in the key suburban district.

Blakeman did slightly better than Lawler among independents with 55% to Hochul’s 37%.
news.summary: The incumbent GOP pol leads with 50% of the vote compared with Conley's 47% in the 17th Congressional District battle, according to the Lawler campaign's internal poll of 400 likely voters.

news.title: Michigan fraudster — once honored by Biden — posed as US ambassador, bank owner to steal $1M from victims to fund lavish lifestyle
news.text:
Call her Money Steal.

A Detroit businesswoman, once honored by President Joe Biden, allegedly posed as a US ambassador and a banker to con several victims out of over $1 million to fund her lavish lifestyle.

Shannon Monet Steel claimed to be the Ambassador to the First Lady of the Central African Republic, a hotel owner and a banker with $350 million in assets to fool her victims in her years-long scheme, federal prosecutors accused, according to the Detroit News on Wednesday.

Steel, 42, was arrested and slapped with fraud charges after allegedly targeting at least eight victims between 2022 and 2026, according to court documents obtained by the outlet.

The Detroit “mogul” curated her online life as a high-rolling, prominent leader, showing off multiple awards and recognitions, her interactions with high-profile politicians and international trips.

Steel is accused of swindling her first victim, a California investor, when she forged a false “Bank confirmation letter” from Deutsche Bank and claimed her own bank, Steel Private Bank, held over 300,000,000 euros.

The falsified letter convinced the victim to wire $200,000 to an escrow account in exchange for a Standby Letter of Credit, the charging documents alleged.

Bank officials later determined the “bank confirmation letter” was a fake.

Officials also discovered Steel Private Bank was registered in the US and wasn’t FDIC insured.

Steel used her self-named “entities” to defraud at least $1.05 million from eight others by assuring them millions in loans from Steel Private Bank but instead “pocketing the good faith escrow funds” from the trusting victims, officials claimed in an Emergency Ex-Parte motion filed with the US District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan on Sept. 10.

Steel used the funds to rent and lease several luxury cars, including a 2022 Maserati Levante and a 2013 Bentley Coupe that cost upwards of $215,000, the outlet reported.

She also paid off credit cards and used $56,000 to rent a home in Northville Township, Mich.

Steel documented her life on social media, promoting herself as Ambassador Steel, wearing merchandise of her fake bank and sharing accomplishments for her false work that earned her national recognition.

“As the newly appointed Ambassador for the First Lady of C.A.R. NGO on a mission to eradicate poverty, I am committed to developing economic stability in the Central African Republic by providing the necessary essentials to its citizens,” Steel wrote on her Shannon Steel Foundation website. 

“My top priority is to represent the country’s history, ideals, and interests. To do so, I am aware of the expectations and will strive to meet them to the best of my ability.

Officials were tipped off to Steel’s fake ambassadorship after a reporter contacted the Department of State trying to verify Steel’s credentials.

In 2024, President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris presented Steel with the Lifetime Presidential Achievement Award. 

Steel shared a poster of the award that labeled her as the CEO of Steel Private Bank, Ambassador and Hedge Fund Owner.

The achievement was “certified by President Biden” as part of the President’s Volunteer Service Awards program and featured photos of Steel, Biden and Harris.

Steel was presented the award without any documentation that she had completed the required 4,000 hours of lifetime volunteer service, the presenter told investigators.

AmeriCorps, the operator of the awards, told investigators Steel being awarded the achievement was inconsistent with program guidelines and she shouldn’t have been given the award based on the information known at the time.

The fraudster boosted her resume when she claimed she acquired and later renovated an Embassy Suites by Hilton hotel for $3,000,000, flipping it to a Wyndham in Southfield, Mich.

Officials discovered the hotel was never granted a certificate of occupancy and never given the authorization to open.

Ramada Worldwide, Inc. won a default judgment against Steel and other defendants for breach of franchise agreement and was awarded $1,558,444.79, according to the court records.

Steel was framed as a con artist with a history of bankruptcies who has used stolen funds to pay off victims who became suspicious of her antics.

“These allegations are only a relevant summary of what Steel is known to be doing to hide and spend criminal proceeds,” Assistant US Attorney K. Craig Welkener wrote. “Her actual efforts are almost certainly more substantial.”
news.summary: A Detroit businesswoman, once honored by President Joe Biden, allegedly posed as a US ambassador and a banker to con several victims out of over $1 million to fund her lavish lifestyle.

news.title: Gen Z isn’t choosing a political party. They’re choosing issues
news.text:
This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th. 

WINDHAM, Maine – As 24-year-old Maya Brooks walked winding roads in rural parts of Maine, a water bottle hooked to her fanny pack and a stack of “lit” on absentee voting and candidates her group has endorsed in hand, she was focused on reaching voters who either haven’t voted in recent years or have shown they’re willing to vote for both parties. 

Mainers frequently cross party lines, as evidenced by the fact that U.S. Sen. Susan Collins is the only GOP senator running for reelection in a state Donald Trump lost in 2024. Maine consistently ranks among the highest in the country for voter turnout, even among young voters, despite having one of the oldest populations in the country. 

That’s led Maine to be viewed as the top state where young voters could sway Senate outcomes in 2026. 

While Brooks canvassed for the state’s largest progressive community action organization, she thought about one of her first interactions knocking doors this cycle. A woman — not much older than herself— told her she probably wouldn’t vote. Whoever she voted for, whatever their party affiliation, she felt it would not make a difference, Brooks recalled.

“I don’t blame her,” she said. While a registered Democrat, Brooks would rather do away with the two-party system altogether. “Politicians aren’t delivering.” 

Generation Z, now roughly 14 to 29 years old, is a growing portion of the electorate with about 50 million eligible voters in the upcoming midterm elections. But these young voters have soured on both parties. 

Younger people have long been more likely to identify as independents, but Gen Z is doing so at a significantly higher rate than any previous generation at the same age. 

Start your day with essential news from Salon.
Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

Being independent does not mean being moderate. Gen Z’s ideological gender gap is driven more by women moving further left than men moving further right. 

“Really, what’s notable is that Gen Z women are the distinct group compared to both their young male counterparts but also to other American women,” said Melissa Deckman, a political scientist who studies the impact of gender, religion, and age on public opinion. “Simply put, Gen Z women are the most liberal and progressive group of voters in America today.” 

A unifier among Gen Z is a belief that the government is failing to protect and address their needs, notably the high cost of living. 

Trump capitalized on that discontent in 2024, making gains with young voters, particularly young men. Now, Trump’s net approval rating is underwater, especially among Gen Z, with 31 percent of young people who voted for the president saying they regret it, according to an August Navigator poll. 

Both parties are trying to remedy mistakes of elections past in the hopes of winning over the Gen Z vote, launching targeted recruitment efforts, hiring more young people and leaning into social media.

No longer taking the youth vote for granted

At a time when many young people were running away from the Democratic Party, Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party, ran to it. 

That is not to say Clayton, who at 25 became the youngest state party chair in the country in 2023 when she ousted an establishment-backed incumbent, has not at times been disappointed.

She wants to see Democrats embrace progressive candidates who win primaries. She wants to get rid of the churn-and-burn cycle of campaigns prioritizing immediate national victories over long-term local sustainability. And she was “so pissed” after Democrats left 44 North Carolina legislative seats uncontested in 2022 that she decided to run for her current role. 

“If you don’t like a party right now, you’re the only one that can change it,” she said in her high-energy cadence.

Clayton got hooked on political work a decade ago, when her county party pushed back on Republicans trying to eliminate the voting site on her college campus. She’s up against similar issues now, after a federal judge ruled against restoring early voting sites on several college campuses in her state earlier this year. 

She has fellows on those campuses to try to turn out the student vote, part of the party’s broader voter protection program, which is in addition to 30 active college chapters and a 100-county, year-round organizing operation. 

“When people look at me and they’re like, ‘Well, young men are leaving the Democratic Party,’ I’m like, ‘Well, let me introduce you then to the leadership that I have right now leading my young Dems, because they are young men,’” Clayton said. “I think that the ability to organize and to help other people see themselves in the party is to also give them that representation.” 

North Carolina Democrats collaborated with Voters of Tomorrow, an entirely Gen Z-led organization seeking to promote political engagement among that demographic, for its national summit in August. Communications director Jessica Siles, 26, said she has seen state parties in particular having more success appealing to young voters. 

“I think in some ways that’s because obviously those ties to the direct local communities are stronger,” Siles said. 

That is borne out in research, which shows relational organizing works because young people trust their neighbors or community networks far more than national parties. Siles sees a sweet spot in engaging Gen Z in events that offer in-person connection in a more social, cultural setting.

That’s an approach being used by the Community Organizing Alliance in Maine, a civic group focused on engaging Black and immigrant voters. Executive director Safiya Khalid, 30, said young people are leading voter registration and education efforts, which include more traditional methods like canvassing, but also events to strengthen community, such as an upcoming concert featuring Somali music, where the alliance will share election-related information to attendees outside the venue. 

The alliance is based in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District. One of the most rural areas east of the Mississippi, it’s an open seat being eyed as consequential for the balance of power in Congress since moderate Democrat Jared Golden is not seeking reelection. 

Another youth-led group in that district, Maine Youth Power, started in 2021 to offer young Mainers clearer paths to engagement in a state with one of the highest median ages. 

“All of our politicians and parties cater towards old people, which is not a bad thing,” said Phoebe Dolan, 28, co-director and one of its founding members. “But it does leave young people often with not a clear sense of a county party that they can join and take leadership in.” 

The nonpartisan organization now reaches roughly 200 young people annually and ahead of the midterms is launching a series of hubs across the state for members to make regional connections. Continuing year-round, the hubs will offer lessons on political history and organizing training, Dolan said. 

In Alabama, GOP chair Scott Stadthagen brought on Brilyn Hollyhand, a 20-year-old content creator from Auburn, who previously advised Trump on youth strategy, to launch Project Future Generation in late July.

The statewide effort to engage teens and young adults in the conservative movement “is not a separate auxiliary group,” Stadthagen said. “We’ve got the young Republicans, the college Republicans. This is creating new Republican members to our county parties.” 

It is a three-pronged approach: a “student strike force” focused on door knocking and registering GOP voters in purple districts, “semester summits” where the party meets with student leaders on campuses, and tours of colleges and high schools. Hollyhand and Stadthagen have ambitions to expand the model to other red states, and eventually swing states.

Comparing the Grand Old Party to a Southern Baptist church, Hollyhand said that without a thriving youth ministry, “when the good ol’ Southern church’s congregation inevitably passes away, the church passes with it.”

The social media factor

When Hollyhand worked for Trump’s campaign, he led the initiative that brought content creators to the 2024 Republican National Convention and urged Trump to make appearances on podcasts and TikToks to reach young people. 

That’s being mimicked by Democrats now. The Democratic National Committee is investing in thousands of content creators to aid wins in 2026 and beyond. Former first lady Michelle Obama launched a “Voting Squad” made up of popular content creators to try to encourage young people to get to the polls. 

More locally, too, campaigns have been leaning on influencers. Independent of Brooks’ job as a senior canvass manager for the Maine People’s Alliance, she regularly posts political content for her more than 85,000 followers on TikTok, an account initially spurred as an outlet to air political rage when Trump got reelected. She was invited as an influencer to one of Maine Democratic gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree’s events.

Despite this focus, research on the effectiveness of influencers is limited. While some studies find that influencers may help boost political awareness among young people, that doesn’t necessarily translate into action. 

“The sort of influence of influencers, if I can be redundant, has been a little bit overstated,” said Alberto Medina, communications manager at Tufts University CIRCLE.

Less than 1 percent of young people said an influencer had been one of their top three motivations to cast a ballot in CIRCLE’s 2024 post-election youth poll. And in its national pre-election poll this year of 5,549 young Americans aged 18–29, social media posts from influencers or celebrities ranked last for the sources of information they turn to for learning about politics and elections.

Most Gen Z voters do get their news on social media, but mostly through posts from advocacy or news organizations, according to the latest survey. 

“Social media algorithms tend to send young men and young women to different places,” said Deckman, who is CEO of the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute. 

She attributes some of the gender divide to the fact that the two demographics are often presented with different informational realities, though it is difficult to quantify. Overall, Gen Z women have been raised with a greater sense of agency, she said, and were brought up politically amid the #MeToo movement and the first Trump presidency, during which his sexist comments shaped public discourse.

In addition to being ideologically divided, young men and women have vastly different beliefs about religion and gender. While young women, and Americans overall, have been shedding religious labels, young men have seen essentially no change in Deckman’s research. Young men are also far more likely to support pronatalism, which the Trump administration has embraced in encouraging families to have more children. 

“No generation is monolithic,” Deckman said. “There definitely are conservative young women. There’s lots of liberal young men. But the trends are such that you’re seeing this gap emerging.” 

Not party but issue motivated

Nelson Dorsey, 20, voted for Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024. Now, the Bowdoin College student is campaigning for Collins, explaining in Brunswick after his early morning football practice that her pitch as an independent voice for the state resonates with him. 

“I’m not necessarily afraid to go across a party line if that means doing what I think is best for the country,” said Dorsey, a registered Republican. “At the time, I was drawn to [Harris’] campaign because she really was drawing on the whole idea of ‘Let’s put politics aside, let’s put our parties aside.’”

Dorsey’s refrain from party loyalty is common among his generation, which is continuing to identify as independent at relatively high rates as they have gotten older, a contrast to older generations who had been less likely to identify as independents over time. 

“You have really a story where Gen Z is really put off by party,” Deckman said. “It’s part of a larger distrust of institutions in society.” 

As Gen Zers struggle to make ends meet, a point of common ground regardless of political leanings, they are seeing the rich get richer and the powerful gain more control. They are united in their concern about the abuse of political and economic power, including the United States’ role in foreign wars and lack of accountability for bad actors named in the Epstein files. 

“Growing up in America at this time, there is a significant lack of hope,” said Katya Fromouth, a 17 year old from Yarmouth, Maine, who thinks she will likely never be able to buy a house and questions what her future will look like because of climate change. “That is the sort of thing that young people need — hope when we are envisioning our future.” 

Fromouth was one of the young Mainers who initially saw hope in former Democratic nominee for Senate Graham Platner, who energized voters with a pitch to rally against corruption regardless of their party affiliation. Platner won over many young people by embracing some of the most polarizing issues at the center of the widening generational divide, such as calling to abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Seeing a candidate for national office with those values was “refreshing and frankly exhilarating,” said Cheyenne Hunt, who had initially endorsed Platner while leading the group Gen Z for Change. 

But after several women came forward alleging sexual misconduct, which he denies, Hunt withdrew her support. She helped support his exes in speaking with media, leading to the publication of an assault allegation in Politico that ultimately ended his campaign. 

While Hunt, founder of Reckoning Action, a nonprofit aiming to combat misogyny, said she received pushback because of the hope Platner inspired, she ultimately sees his swift downfall as evidence of the new kind of politics he had tapped into. 

“Young voters are routinely disappointed with the quality of representation that we’ve been offered,” Hunt said. “They are really ready for a class of representatives that across the board — whether it’s with issues of violence against women, with issues of corruption in general — do not believe that they are above the law and that they deserve special treatment.”

Tufts University CIRCLE has found some links between the issues young voters are focused on and their shifting politics. Those moving to the left care most about healthcare and abortion. Those shifting more conservative are prioritizing immigration and housing.

But regardless of whether their politics are shifting, young people are prioritizing economic issues.

“The centrality of economic issues and of those economic struggles that youth are experiencing is one of the big changes that we’ve been tracking in the last couple of election cycles,” Medina said. 

Young people on both sides think their party needs to change how they talk about the economy. Hollyhand said he wants the GOP to outline solutions, not just offer speeches blaming Democrats. And Clayton said Democrats can’t just rely on the buzzword “affordability.” 

“It’s got to be ‘Here is why the minimum wage is set at $7.25 and here is who’s doing that and who can help make it better,’” she said.

Young people are motivated most to cast a ballot in order to take action on issues they care about. In the Tufts University post-election youth poll from 2024, 46% said that was their top motivator. 

Issues are what Brooks starts with when she speaks to voters canvassing across Maine. As she tries to beat the sun knocking doors into the evening, she asks what matters most to them before sharing what she likes about particular candidates, starting with a local race and not mentioning political affiliations. 

After nearly 40 doors, more than 10,000 steps and three hours, mostly what she’s done is listen. 

“People don’t want to be talked at,” she said. That’s also her message for how the party could improve its chances of courting her generation: “I wish they would just ask.”
news.summary: Young women stand out for their progressive views, but few in the generation are embracing the two-party system

news.title: The Well-Funded Fight to Keep Latinos Voting Republican
news.text:
Alfaro, who’s twenty-seven and the youth director at an evangelical church, has decided to devote his time to turning Latinos into Republican voters. “Maybe you see things on the news, or on social media, but you’re not getting the facts or reliable information—that’s what we want to share with you,” he told Cruz. He introduced himself as a volunteer, but he is the Michigan strategic director for the Libre Initiative, a center-right group that’s affiliated with Charles Koch’s political-action committee Americans for Prosperity. In the past fifteen years, Libre has captured a significant share of the market for Latino voter-turnout operations on the right, with a presence in thirteen states, including all the electoral battlegrounds. Although Libre originated in Texas, a state with more than twelve million Latino residents, the organization chose not to funnel its money into the Senate contest there this fall. Daniel Garza, Libre’s founder and president, said that campaigning statewide for Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general and the Republican candidate for Senate, would have been too expensive, and that the group could have more of an effect on other races. But, “if Paxton loses by a point, two, three points, I won’t be sleeping at night for at least a year,” he told me.
Garza believes that his group can have the greatest influence in Michigan, and Libre has allocated seven figures toward campaigning for Rogers, who lost, in 2024, by fewer than twenty thousand votes. Michigan’s Latino community is small—about six per cent of the state’s population—but there are pockets where it’s highly concentrated. Holland, for instance, a city settled by Dutch Calvinist separatists in 1847, is about a quarter Hispanic. Vionelkis Coen, an immigrant from Cuba and Libre’s grassroots-engagement director in Michigan, pointed out that there was a statue downtown of the city’s founder with his hand on the Bible—a sign, to her, that Holland was culturally “a conservative city.” “I tell people we’re, like, in a bubble,” she said. Since January, Libre has contacted more than a hundred and twenty-five thousand voters in Michigan between phone-banking and door-knocking.
Libre also inhabits a kind of bubble in the electoral ecosystem. It is one of the largest efforts on the right dedicated to motivating Latinos to vote for conservative and libertarian ideals, but its policy goals, such as enacting comprehensive immigration reform and reducing the size of the government, are at odds with President Donald Trump’s efforts to build and execute the largest deportation operation in U.S. history, in addition to other aspects of his agenda, such as his tariff program and the war with Iran. In Grand Rapids, Alfaro introduced me to Miguel Mota, a barbershop owner who voted for Trump but has grown frustrated with him over immigration policy—he’s heard that some of his own clients have been detained. Mota told me that he liked Rogers because he talked about his faith, but Trump was a different matter. “The Bible says, ‘From the abundance of your heart your mouth shall speak,’ ” he said of the President. “You just have to listen to him talk to see what he has inside.” (Rogers declined to be interviewed or clarify whether his position on immigration differed from the President’s.)
In the past, there was a natural place within the G.O.P. for Libre, which is “trying to carve out a more pro-immigrant—in addition, a more pro-Hispanic—wing of the Republicans,” Carlos Odio, a co-founder of Equis Research, which tracks Latino public sentiment, said. “There’s not a space for that now, right? There’s MAGA or bust.” Yet the Party stands to lose Latino voters who coalesced for Trump in 2024; his approval rating among Hispanic voters has fallen as low as twenty-six per cent, according to a recent Times survey. According to Equis, deportations are a significant reason for that drop—though Latinos aren’t particularly enthusiastic about Democrats, either. “Libre is filling a role that the Republican Party is either, one, too stupid to see they need that,” Michael Farage, the ethnic vice-chairman of the Michigan G.O.P., said. “Or, No. 2, they just don’t care. I’m confused, because sometimes you think people aren’t this stupid, but then when you talk to people, then you find out they are that stupid.” (Farage claims to be related to the British politician Nigel Farage; Nigel, through his office, said he had no evidence of their relation.)
Garza, whose parents came from Mexico to the U.S. as migrant farmworkers, told me he finds some of the deportations that the Administration has undertaken difficult to stomach—specifically those involving women and children, and people who have not committed any crimes. “That’s where the rubber hits the road,” he said over dinner at a Mexican restaurant in Grand Rapids. Garza occasionally attends White House events and has spoken to the President, though he has not brought up these concerns to him. “You don’t have all the time in the world to have an extended conversation with the President,” he said, adding that he has discussed the subject with members of the White House’s political staff. “And they see it. They know.” Trump’s firing of Kristi Noem, he added, seemed to be partly a recognition from the White House that the deportation program had gone too far. (The White House did not respond to a request for comment.)
Yet Garza isn’t regretful about helping elect Trump—he voted for him three times and says he’d do it again if he could. Libre helped promote the tax portions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which, among other things, allocated seventy-five billion dollars in funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and sixty-five billion dollars to Customs and Border Protection. On the whole, Garza believes that the MAGA movement has benefitted Latinos more than anything Kamala Harris could have offered, and says that he agrees with Republicans on “eighty to ninety per cent of issues,” including the deportation of immigrants who have committed crimes.
At the same time, Garza hasn’t seen the G.O.P. invest enough money to build on Trump’s gains with Latinos in 2024. Republicans started “taking things for granted, like they just happen automatically,” he said. “This isn’t accidental, man.”
Many of the volunteers I met had arrived in the United States within the past ten years. The atmosphere in the office felt similar to that of a Bible-study group: there were trays of chicken nuggets, mac and cheese, and salad near the entrance, and the organization had bought a birthday cake for one of the volunteers, who said that she wanted to spend the day with Libre, “en familia.” Some people had met Alfaro through his church; others discovered the organization through its nonprofit arm, which has provided community services in places with growing immigrant populations—English lessons, driver’s-education courses, and classes for the U.S. citizenship exam, among others. The group declined to share its operating budget—Americans for Prosperity, one of its backers, has raised about ninety million dollars this year—though Garza clarified that Libre doesn’t receive funds from the Trump family. In some ways, he said, the fact that Koch had been such a prominent and visible donor had shielded the identities of the others.
Garza was born in California, while his parents were working the grape season there. He grew up in Washington and travelled often due to his parents’ itinerant work; by the time he was seventeen, he’d missed so much school that he dropped out and joined his father in the fields, where he saw incidents of Americans taking advantage of the workers. But he also grew skeptical of the labor-rights movement led by Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta. Its members could be inflexible and doctrinaire, he thought; at one point, his parents stopped associating with them because the activists decided to march under the banner of the Virgen de Guadalupe, and they were evangelicals. He later became a police officer, a city councilman in Toppenish, Washington, and a public liaison officer in the George W. Bush White House.
After Garza started Libre, in 2011, as a partner of the Americans for Prosperity network, the backlash from Latinos on the left was swift. By 2015, as Trump launched his Presidential run, Huerta was telling Univision: “They are against the Latino community.” That same year, Hillary Clinton’s campaign officials acknowledged that they needed to figure out a way to match the group’s organizing. “The reality is that Libre is VERY good,” Clinton’s national political director wrote in an e-mail to leadership. “They have finally figured out the FOX approach to Latinos.” Albert Morales, a former Hispanic-engagement director for the Democratic National Committee, and a friend of Garza’s, remembers, after Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico in 2017, seeing images of Libre volunteers greeting victims at Florida airports with merchandise. Meanwhile, he said, Democrats in Florida, such as Senator Bill Nelson, who was running for reëlection, had done little outreach to Latinos. “I remember the campaign manager telling me, ‘You’re the one who requested this call.’ And I knew then, this one’s gone,” Morales said. (Nelson’s former campaign manager called this claim “inaccurate and laughable.”)
Garza told me that other Latinos often accuse him of catering to white people to earn their praise, but this doesn’t bother him. Even when Huerta came out against him, he said he was neither surprised nor dismayed. “It’s not like I’m fighting for white people,” he told me. “I’m fighting for my own people—and sometimes white people get it right, goddamit!” But he bristles at the suggestion that he uses Latinos to advance Republican causes. That was the impression that Eric Kas, a voter in Grand Rapids, got when Garza and a few Libre canvassers knocked at his door. Kas had questions for the group, such as whether Garza was paying people to canvass, whether Libre was a Republican group, and what the “Hispanic connection” to Mike Rogers could possibly be.
Also: “Do you accept money from super PACs?” Kas asked.
“So,” Garza said, “we are a PAC.”
Kas chuckled; the two had a spirited debate over the influence of money in politics before parting ways. But, after Kas looked into the group and saw that it was linked to the Koch family, he told me his first impression was reinforced. “It just made sense that this was why a group of Latinos may want to walk through our neighborhood to share information by Mike Rogers,” he said. When I relayed Kas’s comments to Garza, he found them insulting. “We’re not the property of the left,” he said.
In an interview in August, El-Sayed said that he was formalizing his campaign’s outreach to Latinos; since then, he has hired a Latino-outreach director. “Our party has talked about being a big tent, but we organize people by putting them on the outside of the tent, and then we go and pander to them on particular issues, rather than bringing them to the center tentpole around what it looks like to afford their life,” he said. El-Sayed has campaigned on abolishing ICE, but Marroquin, who hosted a meet and greet for him, said that he would do well to focus on cost-of-living issues. “Those are everyday issues,” Marroquin said. “They transcend all identities.”
Somos Votantes, an advocacy organization with a nonprofit arm, is attempting to adapt the Libre playbook for the left. (The PAC is supported by the Soros family.) Melissa Morales, the organization’s founder and president, told me over coffee in Washington, D.C., that Republicans have been smart in “recognizing that people aren’t interested in an ideological victory; they’re interested in a system that works, or a system that’s meeting their needs in the immediate.” A former union organizer, Morales recently announced that Somos is investing three million dollars into campaigning efforts in Michigan. The nonprofit arm recently announced a program through which Michigan residents could apply for up to a thousand dollars to pay their utility bills, partly inspired by the stimulus checks that Trump issued during the COVID-19 lockdown. Morales recalled that, after her father cashed his check, he told her that it was the most money he’d ever held in his hands.
In August, at a Somos Votantes event at a Latino community center in Kalamazoo, Michigan, the group announced its utility-bill initiative and gave out free backpacks, food, and haircuts for back-to-school season. Cynthia Portillo, a single mother of six, told me that she sat out the 2024 election because she saw an ad stating that Harris wanted to allow trans children to use the bathroom of their choice. Portillo said that she didn’t know much about the upcoming Senate race, and wished that the event could offer more information about it (because the event was under Somos’s nonprofit banner, campaign materials were not allowed). But she did plan to fill out an application for the check.
Calling Democrats Communists isn’t new, but it seems to be a safer bet for a Republican in 2026 than breaking with the President over immigration. (After a Latina Republican incumbent in Miami cut an ad saying that Trump’s policies had gone too far, the President amplified criticisms of her on social media.) In Michigan, Garza said he wouldn’t recommend that Rogers distance himself from Trump to win over Latinos. “Maybe he will show an attraction to Latino voters, but you’re going to lose so much more in the white base that it’s going to offset whatever you gain,” he said. “He would lose in the end.”
Garza believes that Libre still has room to influence the G.O.P., and says that his group has prevailed on certain policy debates over school choice, lowering taxes, driving up energy production, and expanding telehealth access for Latinos in rural areas. But “ultimately, they chose Donald Trump, not Daniel Garza, to run the country,” he said. “And so Donald Trump gets to decide what the policies are at the end of the day.”
Albert Morales said that if Democrats win the midterms, Trump will become a lame duck—which could give Libre an opening to influence the 2028 primary. “I can see a world where they come out early in support of Rubio for the nomination—and just think of the machine they have in place for him when that primary begins,” he said. “The lights are still going to be on at Libre on November 4th, whereas some of our organizations, who are running ads right now and have field campaigns going—they’re going to shut down,” Morales added. “It’s just the way we operate.” ◆
news.summary: Amid deportations and Trump’s lagging popularity, one Koch-backed group has recruited Michigan Latinos to reach more than a hundred thousand voters for Mike Rogers.

news.title: Trump vowed to lower gas prices. His backers in Alaska are not buying it.
news.text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska — Americans have had it with fuel prices. Just ask Trump voters in Alaska.

The average cost of a gallon of gas is more than $5 statewide. Diesel prices hit their highest-ever recorded level in September. Those economic conditions are leaving some Trump voters in the state fed up and giving rise to an optimism among Democrats that former congresswoman Mary Peltola could unseat incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in November.

 Source: OPIS, a Dow Jones company; Chart: Carson Elm-Picard / MS NOW

“It’s hard out here. Simple,” said Calvin Mitchell, a 41-year-old security guard from Anchorage who voted for President Donald Trump in each of the past three presidential elections.

 It’s hard out here. Simple.”—Calvin Mitchell

“I can’t go see my daughter out of state, and we’re not buying as many groceries, and we’re not really doing anything fun or entertainment unless it’s free,” said Gayle Michaelson, 48, a paralegal and three-time Trump voter.

What would she tell the president? “I would tell him what he initially told the voters is BS — that these prices weren’t supposed to be so high — and look what’s happened.”

 What he initially told the voters is BS — that these prices weren’t supposed to be so high — and look what’s happened.”—Gayle Michaelson

Trump decisively won Alaska in the past three elections, beating Hillary Clinton by about 15 points in 2016, Joe Biden by about 10 points in 2020 and Vice President Kamala Harris by about 13 points in 2024.

But the skyrocketing cost of diesel fuel, which is disproportionately integral to the everyday lives of Alaskans, is among the factors that are putting Sullivan’s seat in danger from his Democratic challenger, Peltola.

“A lot of people are going to look at the other way, because a lot of trucking, especially myself, truck drivers are owner-ops ... they can’t afford the diesel,” said Meffy Tagalu, a trucker and three-time Trump voter. Like Alaska’s fishing industry, which is a cornerstone of the state’s economy, trucking is particularly susceptible to diesel price fluctuations, currently due to the war with Iran.

“We need to get out of that war and fix all the prices. You know, we’re hurting really bad,” Tagalu said, putting the blame squarely at Trump’s feet.

“Everybody that voted for him” is starting to turn their backs on him, Tagalu said.

Not everyone.

Carl Cleveland is a Marine veteran who voted for Trump three times and has voted for Sullivan in the past. The way things are going has left him disillusioned with the American political system.

 Everybody’s just fed up with the current system.”—Carl Cleveland

“Everybody’s just fed up with the current system,” said the 47-year-old. “We work our ass off to keep food on the table with a roof over our heads, and these guys go to D.C. … They go down there and just forget about us, and that’s how Sullivan was, or is right now,” he said.

Cleveland did not want to reveal whether he is supporting Sullivan or Peltola in the midterms, but he said that when it comes down to his decision, “It’s just the price at the pump. You got to look at that.”

In 2020, Sullivan dominated his re-election bid, beating independent Al Gross by more than 12 points. But in August’s open primary, Peltola beat Sullivan by about 8 points, a signal that Alaskans may be primed to elect a Democrat to the U.S. Senate for the first time since Mark Begich in 2008.

Despite deep frustration with the president, many of these Trump voters said they are not swayed in their support from Sullivan.

 [Trump] doesn’t do anything he says. He’s a lot of rhetoric and very little action.”—Jason McNulty

“I’m going to have to go with Sullivan just because Peltola’s record doesn’t prove out,” said Jason McNulty, a three-time Trump voter who said he is “done with Trump” and that the president “doesn’t do anything he says. He’s a lot of rhetoric and very little action.”

news.title: The Patriot Post® · Toward the Final Stretch — and Beyond
news.text:
Haven’t we seen this movie before? Voters, weary of a Republican president whose foreign or domestic policies don’t seem to be delivering as promised, seem on the verge of a massive rejection of his party.

Polls show Democrats surging. The generic ballot — which party’s candidates would you favor for the House of Representatives? — shows Democrats far ahead of Republicans. Statewide polls show Democrats ahead in large states that had voted Republican for president and threatening incumbents in historically Republican states such as Kansas and Nebraska.

That’s pretty much the picture today. Donald Trump’s job approval has slipped below 40%, below his numbers at the end of September 2018 and similar to George W. Bush’s in September 2006.

Republicans trail in the generic vote by about as much as in 2018 and by wider margins in 2006.

All of which provides a strong basis for the professional prognosticators’ predictions that Democrats will overturn the Republicans’ current narrow majority in the House and some justification for those who say they have a majority chance of gaining the four seats that would give them a majority in the Senate. 

But there are a couple of caveats here. Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini points out that polls in the last four congressional elections have understated Republicans’ actual election performance by wide margins in the summer, then narrowed in the fall. But this year, there is little sign of such narrowing yet.

But perhaps the polls are consistently understating Republican support, as analyst Nate Silver says they have in the last three presidential elections. Many pollsters report it’s much harder to reach Republican respondents, who tend to mistrust media pollsters.

And this year, many Republicans seem unhappy with the president and his party. Does that mean they’re just unwilling to be polled or that they will skip voting as well? No one knows the answer.

And no one knows the answer to the question posed by Robert Redford’s character in the movie “The Candidate” when he wins the election: “What do we do now?” No one seems to know for sure what Democrats will do if they win majorities in both houses. A Democratic Senate is unlikely to confirm any Trump appointee to the Supreme Court and probably to any federal court, and would likely extract concessions from any nominee to a high policy position — unless Pennsylvania’s John Fetterman denies Democrats their 51st vote.

Democratic majorities might try to cabin Trump’s power to set tariffs, but they won’t be able to change underlying trade statutes and must depend on the courts to decide, as they have already in some cases, that those laws don’t justify Trump’s actions.

Democrats may also try to end U.S. military operations against Iran, which, in any case, have been erratic. But they may not be able to. Bush was able to execute his successful surge strategy in Iraq, despite majority opposition in both houses after Democrats’ victories in the off-year elections in 2006.

One gets little sense from the campaign dialogue what Democratic majorities would aim to do on other policies. Their candidates decry high gas prices and inflation generally. But they’re unlikely to revert to the Biden administration’s policy, prompted by the COVID-19 pandemic, of vastly expanding federal spending, which resulted in 9% inflation in 2022 and remained a continuing liability for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris in 2024.

There’s a general impulse in the Democratic Party to see the working class as its core constituency and to respond to its presumed needs with economic redistribution. That’s the lesson Democrats take from Franklin Roosevelt and the rich literature inspired by his New Deal.

But the impulse is outdated. The white college graduate voters who now dominate Democratic primaries and fundraising may indulge the Marxist and progressive presumption that the working class is especially morally worthy, but they can hardly help observing that blue-collar workers have been voting increasingly Republican even before Trump rode down his escalator.

Indeed, as economist and former Sen. Phil Gramm has shown, the United States already has economic redistribution policies locked into place, so that the bottom 60% of income earners are eligible for government transfer payments, raising them to average income levels.

In those circumstances, Biden’s major push toward redistribution was his frequent proposals (sometimes overruled, like Trump’s tariffs, by the courts) for forgiveness of college and graduate student loans. The beneficiaries of those loans were not only the gender studies majors looking for adjunct work but also the gaggles of college and university administrators subsidized by those programs.

It’s interesting that the Biden administration, staffed not only at the top but throughout with Obama administration veterans, did not seek a highly visible overhaul of health care financing.

They surely remember the political price they paid for Obamacare. Passed only by parliamentary legerdemain in the face of adverse polling, it saw Republicans gain 64 House seats in the 2010 off-year election. That was the biggest off-year gain for either party since Bill Clinton broke Republicans’ lock on the presidency in 1992 and Newt Gingrich broke Democrats’ lock on the House in 1994.

Defenders of Obamacare may respond that Republicans’ attempts to repeal it were unpopular and were defeated by John McCain’s vote in 2018. But tying together the broad opposition to Obamacare during Barack Obama’s tenure with the broad opposition to Obamacare repeal during Trump’s is the fact that large majorities of the public, for all their grumblings, are content with their current health care financing and oppose any attempts to take it away.

That’s something Democrats may want to consider when they see young Democratic Socialists of America support Bernie Sanders’ Medicare for All proposal. By definition, it would eliminate the arrangements most Americans have made and are content with. Lots of voters are not going to like that.

American voters generally, and Democratic politicians in particular, tend to look to government to cure various ills. In that perspective, you can argue — and certainly public opinion polls would suggest most people would — that the nation’s performance in this first quarter of the 21st century has been suboptimal.

But the mostly unanticipated performance of the private sector has been better, in technological devices and communication and in fracking technology, which has made the U.S. once again the world’s greatest oil producer, as it was at the outset of World War II. Elon Musk has outperformed the heavily regulated Detroit Three in making a profitable business of building electric cars and has outperformed government-run NASA at producing reusable space rockets.

Looking back over the century so far, the historian Niall Ferguson admits, “My prophetic vision of decline and fall 25 years ago clearly has not been fulfilled. In relative terms, America is still Number One by any measure except maybe the number of robots.” That despite the disappointments and demerits of successive administrations and Congresses. Whether the Democrats sweep the off-year elections next month or the Republicans once again outpoll the polls, the winners — and losers — might want to keep that perspective in mind.

news.title: Hakeem Jeffries says 'sky's the limit' for Ocasio-Cortez in 2028
news.text:
WASHINGTON – House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries isn’t ready to make a 2028 pick yet, but says “the sky's the limit” for fellow New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive who has acknowledged she’s considering a presidential bid or a U.S. Senate run.

“Alex has done a tremendous job championing a whole host of issues of great importance to both New Yorkers and to the nation," Jeffries said. “I think the sky's the limit for her in terms of how she decides to move forward. She's going to have to make that decision, you know, at some point. And, you know, it will be big news when she does.”

Ocasio-Cortez, 36, has been weighing whether to seek the presidency or the U.S Senate seat that Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, 75, has held since 1999.

The New York City congresswoman recently completed a listening tour of upstate New York, stoking anticipation that she could challenge Schumer, if the five-term senator who has repeatedly drawn the ire of progressives decides to run again.

Asked in an interview if he thought Schumer should run for reelection – and whether Ocasio-Cortez should compete – Jeffries told USA TODAY he was staying in his lane as House Democratic leader.

He said Schumer had "been a great partner," who he's worked with for a long time. "He'll have to make decisions in the aftermath of this midterm election. I know right now he's focused on trying to take back the Senate,” Jeffries said.

More: How AOC is upending norms around motherhood and political candidacy

Ocasio-Cortez had a 66% favorability rating among New York Democrats in a recent Quinnipiac University poll. Her overall approval rating in the state stood at 46% — compared to Schumer, who had a 34% statewide approval rating. The longtime lawmaker had a 56% favorability rating among Democrats alone.

A possible presidential candidate

In presidential polling, Ocasio-Cortez, also known as AOC, is one of only a handful of potential candidates who has been able to hit double digits.

She received 12% support from Democrats in a Harvard-Harris poll taken in late September, ranking just ahead of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who had 11% support, and behind California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who received 17%.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris led the field with 38% support among surveyed Democrats.

Speaking to the New York Times last month, Ocasio-Cortez was candid about a possible run.

“It’s very all or nothing,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “If I were to run in this cycle, and not win, I would be done.”

Jeffries, who has his eye on the House speakership, said he was not “getting involved in the presidential sweepstakes right now." He told USA TODAY his focus was on winning control of the House.

“I think it's going to be a big field. We'll have some great candidates. Maybe one or two from the House, we’ll see,” Jeffries told USA TODAY.

He said the Democratic Party's presidential primary "will be a robust discussion, so we can actually complete the job, which we have to complete in November of 2028, so we can end the error of MAGA extremism in the United States of America once and for all.”

news.title: Ms Rachel builds sprawling media empire while shelling out thousands to progressive candidates
news.text: The popular children's YouTuber Rachel Accurso has spent over $22,000 backing Democratic and progressive candidates since 2024, while her toddler-facing brand has expanded into Netflix, Penguin Random House and the toy aisles of Target. Better known as "Ms. Rachel," the online star has cemented herself as the face of a multimillion-dollar children’s entertainment empire. The former New York City preschool educator, who sings nursery rhymes and teaches language to more than 21 million YouTube subscribers, has also become one of the most politically outspoken figures in her arena, drawing scrutiny for her positions on the Israel-Hamas war, racial issues and various Trump administration immigration policies. "Ms. Rachel is a children's entertainer, a personality that spawned from the YouTube ecosystem and has now become a fixture alongside other big preschool brands like Sesame Street or Bluey or Cocomelon," James Zahn, editor-in-chief of "The Toy Book," told Fox News Digital. "For families that have ‘littles,’ as she would say, she's a part of daily life at this point," he added. MS RACHEL URGES 'EVERY WEALTHY WHITE CELEBRITY' TO MATCH MACKLEMORE'S DONATION TO PALESTINIAN CAUSES Accurso, 43, launched her YouTube channel in 2019 after finding few media resources for her son, who had a speech delay as a toddler. Her channel quickly surged in popularity, leading her to create "Songs for Littles," a recurring series in which Accurso — clad in her signature pink shirt, overalls and headband — performs a mix of classic and original children's songs for infants, toddlers and preschoolers. Her rise to fame has made her one of the most commercially significant figures in American children’s media — and, at the same time, one of the most politically outspoken. According to federal records, Accurso has donated roughly $22,500 to various Democratic and progressive candidates since 2024, and has made headlines for her outspoken stances on the Israel-Hamas war and other politically charged topics. MOMS FOR LIBERTY CO-FOUNDER WARNS PARENTS ABOUT MS RACHEL’S POLITICAL ACTIVISM, ‘NOT MR ROGERS’ Accurso has managed to secure deals with Netflix, Penguin Random House Books and Spin Master Toys. "These companies look at it as: if an entertainer doesn't blur real life into the content, that tends to make things a little bit safer," Zahn said. Earlier this year, Spin Master debuted a line of toys in collaboration with Accurso — marking yet another feather in her cap as her brand hit the shelves of big-box stores such as Target and Amazon. "In the years leading up to the announcement of Ms. Rachel's toy deal with Spin Master, there was a bidding war," Zahn said. "So toy and game makers knew that she was a personality with a ton of reach that was worth talking to." MS RACHEL CONFRONTED ON ACCUSING ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' IN PARK INTERACTION WITH PODCASTER "I distinctly remember at Toy Fair New York knowing that Ms. Rachel was in the building — not in character, but she was taking meetings," he continued. "And eventually the question became, within the industry: who is going to get the Ms. Rachel toys?" The line features a variety of toys geared toward both learning and entertainment, with Ms. Rachel personified as a toy-version of herself in several sets. Her reach has also spread from the online ecosystem into both mainstream and print media after she landed partnerships with Netflix in 2025 and book publisher Penguin Random House in 2024. "The Ms. Rachel deal with Netflix brings her show to kids who may not otherwise have access to it," Zahn said. "Even though we're in such a screen-heavy world, not every family allows their kids to operate on YouTube." KAROL MARKOWICZ: MS. RACHEL SAID, 'I AM POLITICAL.' PARENTS SHOULD TAKE HER AT HER WORD "When we think of media, and we think how digital it is, the analog basis — especially for the younger kids — is very, very key," he added, referring to Accurso’s line of children’s books. The multi-pronged licensing approach to Accurso’s brand marks a significant — and somewhat unprecedented — shift in children’s entertainment, in which influencers reign in spaces traditionally reserved for mainstream media. "Today's children, even from the youngest ages, don't just want to watch a television program," David Kleeman, senior vice president of global trends for Dubit, told Fox News Digital. "They want to be part of the media that they consume. They want to play with it. They want to act it out. They want to wear the clothing." As Accurso’s persona continues to reach into every aspect of a child’s life — from the shows they watch to the toys they play with — Kleeman emphasizes the need for the individual behind the brand to maintain a level of trust with the parents choosing to keep her content in the hands of their children. MS RACHEL CLAIMS CELEBRITIES SILENT ON GAZA WOULD ‘PROBABLY’ SPEAK IF CHILDREN ‘WERE WHITE’ "Parents have always looked to media as a support for what they’re doing with their kids," Kleeman said. "We tell parents, ‘You’re your child’s first teacher.’ That petrifies a lot of parents, so [they] look for ways to supplement what [they’re] able to do for your child." However, Accurso’s public politics have made her children’s education brand synonymous with hot-button political issues, such as the ongoing Israel-Hamas war and tensions surrounding Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She's also put some money behind prominent Democrats. In 2024, the day after then-President Joe Biden dropped out of the ongoing election and endorsed Vice President Kamala Harris as his Democratic successor, Accurso donated $250 to the Harris Victory Fund. HOW MS RACHEL'S POLITICAL ACTIVISM IS SPARKING PUSHBACK FROM PARENTS In the days following, she contributed an additional $750 in funds to Harris for President and the Harris Victory Fund, according to Federal Election Commission records. By September 2024, Accurso had shelled out an additional $2,000 in donations to Harris’ campaign — bringing the total to $3,000 in campaign contributions, records show. One year later, Accurso made a $5,000 donation to Cameron Kasky’s New York congressional campaign, according to NYC Campaign Finance Board records obtained by Fox News Digital. She was issued a $1,500 refund from Kasky’s campaign on the same day. Kasky — a survivor of the 2018 high school mass shooting in Parkland, Florida — ran on a platform centered around abolishing ICE, ending military funding to Israel and stricter gun-violence laws. He ultimately dropped out of the race in January 2026 following a trip to the West Bank, in which he cited a new focus on stopping "settler violence" in the region, according to an X post. Throughout 2026, campaign finance records show Accurso has spent $12,000 on various New York races with candidates of similar views. MS RACHEL DEFENDS 'AWESOME' MAMDANI AMID 9/11 MEMORIAL CONTROVERSY, SAYS HE'S VICTIM OF ISLAMOPHOBIC ATTACKS The children’s educator donated $5,000 to former New York State Assemblymember Yuh-Line Niou’s state Senate campaign, plus an additional $3,500 to Democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier and $4,500 to former New York City Comptroller Brad Lander. While Niou failed to win in the primaries earlier this year, both Chevalier and Lander won the Democratic nominations for their respective congressional campaigns. All three candidates have strongly campaigned on platforms that are critical of both Israel and ICE. Federal Election Commission records also show Accurso gave $3,000 to Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan Senate campaign in July, marking yet another contribution to a controversial candidate who has repeatedly alleged Israel is committing a "genocide" in Gaza. DAVID MARCUS: IN BOOMING DETROIT, VOTERS SKEPTICAL OF SOCIALISM SNAKE OIL "I am political," she said in March, describing her opposition to Immigration and Customs Enforcement. She has been similarly direct about the Israel-Hamas war, drawing scrutiny in 2025 after appearing in a video referring to Palestinian photojournalist Motaz Azaiza as her "friend" — days before Azaiza admitted to withholding footage of Israeli hostages being beaten by a crowd in Gaza on Oct. 7, 2023. "There isn't a lot of precedent when it comes to a kid's entertainer making comments outside of their content that rub people the wrong way — or in some cases the right way," Zahn said. The YouTuber’s checkbook tells a similar story, with her net worth reportedly estimated at around $50 million. Last year, Forbes’ 2025 Top Creators List ranked Accurso at No. 20 with a whopping $23 million in annual earnings. The dollar figures — and subsequent brand deals — signify an apparent fan separation between Ms. Rachel as a brand and Accurso as a public figure. "It's always an issue when you have a presenter who is basically presenting as themselves," Kleeman told Fox News Digital. "Mr. Rogers just was ‘Mr. Rogers.’ There was no character or artifice there. Ms. Rachel has created ‘Ms. Rachel,’ as opposed to Rachel Accurso." "Viewers often have a problem separating that real-life person from the character," he added. MS RACHEL CLAIMS 'NO ONE NEEDS A BILLION DOLLARS,' ENDORSES DEMOCRATIC PROGRESSIVES ABDUL EL-SAYED, CORI BUSH The sentiment was echoed by Zahn, who suggests that Accurso’s high-profile political stances are doing little to deter brands from signing her YouTube persona. "Companies can take multiple approaches, as we've seen with other celebrity controversies," Zahn said. "They can choose to back the celebrity, they can push back from the celebrity, they can distance themselves from it, or they can say nothing at all. And sometimes saying nothing at all is what it really needs." While parents may be keyed into Accurso’s views on topics such as Gaza and gender representation, Kleeman argues that as long as the content creator keeps politics out of her educational materials, she will likely feel little pushback from both brands and fans. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "I think she's been very careful to keep what she puts out to children focused on the child development, on the learning, on the play," Kleeman told Fox News Digital. "I think that Netflix or any channel that’s carrying content that’s being presented by a real person is going to have to balance how well that person is conveying what it is they’re transmitting to kids — the specific children’s content, not the things that go around it." news.summary: Ms. Rachel has donated thousands to progressive political candidates as her popular children's education brand expanded into Netflix, Penguin Random House and Target.
